targets.why: Uses Box-Jenkins time-series modeling and earlier Box-Newbold spurious-model experience to analyze autocorrelated regression errors.

evidence.quote: We find it very curious that whereas virtually every textbook on econometric methodology contains explicit warnings of the dangers of autocorrelated errors, this phenomenon crops up so frequently in well-respected applied work.
Despite this, many papers still appear with equations having such symptoms and these equations are presented as though they have some worth.

targets.why: Criticizes applied econometric practice that reports high-R2 regressions with autocorrelated residuals and treats them as meaningful despite invalid tests.

evidence.quote: The point of view we intend to take is that of the statistical time series analyst, rather than the more classic econometric approach.

Finally, in sect. 5, we re-emphasize the importance of error specification and draw a distinction between the philosophy of time series analysis and econometric methodology, which we feel to be of great importance to practitioners of the latter.

evidence.quote: It is quite clear from these simulations that if one’s variables are random walks, or near random walks, and one includes in regression equations variables which should in fact not be included, then it will be the rule rather than the exception to find spurious relationships.
It is also clear that a high value for R2 or R2, combined with a low value of d, is no indication of a true relationship.

thesis.text: Regressions among independent or highly autocorrelated/nonstationary economic time series, especially levels or random walks, often yield spurious significant relationships with high R2 and low Durbin-Watson values, so such equations are mis-specified and their usual significance tests are invalid.

sections.summary: Introduces the puzzle of regressions with high R2 or corrected R2 but very low Durbin-Watson d, links it to autocorrelated errors, and sets the paper's focus on invalid significance tests and spurious relationships.
sections.title: The Spurious Regression Problem

type.reason: It is a methodological econometrics paper critiquing spurious regression and supporting the argument with simulation experiments.

corrections.reason: The paper is organized into five numbered sections (1 Introduction, 2 Some results in time series analysis, 3 How nonsense regressions can arise, 4 Some simulation results, 5 Discussion and conclusion), but the draft records only a single section, and its title "The Spurious Regression Problem" is not a section heading used anywhere in the paper. The section inventory is therefore both mis-titled and incomplete; I cannot reliably reconstruct the missing summaries.
